health.summary: Liveness and the tier the node is talking to
health.because: The edge node polls this to decide whether it is online, in which case the UI must not claim a write reached the cloud. Nothing here may be cached.
health.notes: Deliberately online-only: a stale answer to “am I connected?” is worse than no answer, because the whole point of the call is to tell the screen whether a write reached the cloud.

listPatients.because: Reads are served from the edge replica, so the desk keeps working with the uplink down. A cached page of results is better than an empty one, and the screen stamps how old it is.

createPatient.because: A registration at a desk over a dead uplink still has to happen: the patient is in front of you. The write is queued with an idempotency key and replayed; the MRN comes from a block already reserved to this node.

getPatient.because: Served from the local replica; a record opened during an outage is the record the desk needs most.

updatePatient.because: Two desks can both correct a name or an age. Different fields merge automatically; the same field is offered to a person, because one of the two is wrong and only the patient knows which.

updatePatientContact.summary: Correct a phone number, address or next of kin
updatePatientContact.because: Contact details change constantly and relatives answer the phone. The same field on two nodes is a conflict for a person to settle, never a silent overwrite: the wrong number on a discharge call is a patient who cannot be reached.

listPatientDuplicates.because: Duplicate detection is a rule set, not a boolean: the response carries the evidence (matching name, phone, date of birth, branch) so a person can decide, and the thresholds are tunable in Setup.

listAppointments.because: Reads come from the replica, so the calendar draws during an outage. Bookings made offline are merged on drain and the screen marks which rows are still local.

createAppointment.because: The branch where the patient is standing owns the slot. If two branches book the last slot, the origin that took the booking keeps it and the other is refused with the alternative times — a booking desk that cannot say who has the slot is worse than a busy signal.

updateAppointment.because: Slots are exclusive: one appointment holds one slot. A reschedule is a claim on the new slot and a release of the old one, in that order, so a failed second step never leaves two appointments holding one slot.

checkInAppointment.because: Check-in is what puts a patient into the queue, and it is the event the queue board and the bill both read. It is exclusive: the second check-in of the same token is refused rather than duplicated, because a patient called twice is a patient seen once.

claimBed.summary: Claim a bed for an admission
claimBed.because: A bed holds one patient. Two nodes admitting into the same bed is not a merge — the second arrival needs another bed, so the claim is refused and the admission desk is told which beds are free.

createAdmission.because: An admission is an event with a time and an author. Two events written on two nodes are two events and both belong in the record, so nothing is merged away.

createObservation.because: A set of vitals is a measurement at a time. Two sets are two measurements; both belong on the chart, and the early-warning score is computed on the server that holds the chart.

createNursingNote.because: Notes are the record of what was seen and done: nothing merges and nothing is overwritten, so the note is appended and the author and time are part of it.

signDose.summary: Sign a dose at the bedside
signDose.because: A dose is given once. Two nodes signing the same slot is a double-dose risk: the first signature stands and the second is refused with the reason. A controlled drug also carries a witness, which is why the audit requirement here is not the usual one.

createInvoice.because: Invoices are reversed and reissued, never edited — so two nodes produce two documents and a credit note rather than one merged figure. The number comes from a block reserved to this node, which is what keeps two branches from issuing the same receipt.

recordPayment.because: Money received is a fact with a counter and a time. Two receipts are two payments, and the day-end sheet has to reconcile against a physical drawer, so nothing merges.

appendAuditEntry.because: The ledger of who did what is the one thing that must never be merged away, and it is written on the node that performed the action. An audit entry that waits for a connection is still an audit entry.

listNumberBlocks.summary: Number blocks reserved to this node
listNumberBlocks.because: A node draws MRNs and invoice numbers from ranges reserved to it, which is what lets it register a patient with no uplink and still not collide with another branch. The call must reach the cloud tier: a node that cannot reserve a block cannot start a day offline, and the UI has to say so before the uplink fails rather than after.
listNumberBlocks.notes: Deliberately online-only: an offline node with no reserved block may read and queue, but it may not mint identifiers.

createIncomeVoucher.because: The counter that took the money is the only place that knows it was taken. Queue it, and the day book shows the receipt as awaiting sync until it lands, which is how a drawer and a ledger stay reconciled without a phone call.

createExpenseVoucher.because: Accounts records what it paid when it paid it, and the approval ladder is checked before the voucher leaves the desk — a payment that cannot be approved is refused at the source rather than found missing a signature a week later.

submitClaim.because: The claim is raised where the patient was treated, which is the only place that has the file and the discharge summary. Queue it: a claim desk that cannot raise a claim offline stops admitting payer patients the moment the link drops.

recordClaimResponse.because: The remittance advice arrives at a desk with a telephone and a spreadsheet, so the answer is typed where it is read. Queue it, and the claim shows the answer as awaiting sync until it lands rather than pretending the money is settled.

createCommissionPayout.because: A payout is money leaving for a clinical decision made weeks earlier, and the account that pays it is where the cheque is written. Queue it, and the run shows the voucher as awaiting sync until the bank confirms it.

listStaff.because: The roster is read at 06:50 by whoever is handing over, and a roster that needs the cloud to open is a roster that is wrong exactly when the link is down. Serve it from the branch replica and stamp how old the page is.

createStaffRecord.because: A new joiner is recorded at the desk where the paperwork was signed, which may well be the branch with the worse uplink. Queue it: the employee number is drawn from the node’s own block, so the record is complete when it is written rather than when it reaches the cloud.

updateStaffRecord.because: Corrections to a designation, a phone number or a licence expiry happen at the desk and are false for as long as they sit on one node. Queue them with the field list and the version, so two desks correcting different fields merge and two correcting the same field are offered both values.

recordAttendancePunch.because: The punch happens at a door in this building, to a reader mounted on the wall, and the door does not care whether the uplink is up. It is queued from the branch node in the order the reader saw it, because two punches out of order are two punches nobody can pair into a shift.

recordAttendanceAdjustment.summary: Correct an attendance day by hand
recordAttendanceAdjustment.because: A card left in a pocket and a reader that died are both real, and the payroll that runs on bad attendance pays somebody the wrong amount. The adjustment is a record of its own naming the supervisor, the reason and the time — it never overwrites the punch it corrects.

createLeaveRequest.because: Leave is applied for in the ward office by somebody who is about to be short-staffed, and the ward needs the application on the board whether or not the cloud can be reached. Queue it and show it as awaiting approval, which is a state the roster can already cope with.

decideLeaveRequest.summary: Approve or refuse a leave application
decideLeaveRequest.because: The decision is made by a person looking at a roster, and it has to reach the ward the same way the application did. A refusal carries its reason and an approval carries who covers the shift, because that is the sentence the roster and the payroll both read.

runPayroll.summary: Compute a month’s payroll for a branch
runPayroll.because: A payroll run is arithmetic over attendance that already exists on this node, so it is computed here and queued as a whole: the lines, the totals and the cut-off it was computed from. Nothing about it needs the cloud to be reachable at the minute somebody presses the button.

approvePayrollRun.summary: Approve a payroll run for payment
approvePayrollRun.because: This is the signature that releases money to every employee of a branch at once, and it is the one action in this module that may not be taken on a disconnected device: an approval that exists only in a queue is a signature nobody can verify against the ledger, and payroll is the one place where “probably approved” is not a state.
approvePayrollRun.notes: Deliberately online-only: the approval is what the bank file is generated from, and a queued approval would let a branch pay a month the cloud ledger does not yet know about — which is the one discrepancy that cannot be reconciled afterwards without asking a person to repay money.

listVitalEvents.summary: Read the day’s births and deaths
listVitalEvents.because: The register is read at the desk where a family is standing, and the report that summarises it is read by the branch that wrote it. Serve the day from the node that recorded it, cached, rather than from a cloud page that may be a shift behind.

recordBirth.because: A birth happens at three in the morning with one midwife on the floor, and the register number comes from this node’s own block so the entry is complete when it is written. Queue it: the notification to the registrar can wait for an uplink, but the record cannot wait for one.

recordDeath.because: The death record is written by the clinician who was there, in the hour it happened, and the mortuary reads it before the body moves. It is queued as an immutable event: a certificate number issued against a cause, and a referral to the police recorded with its station and time.

openVisitorPass.because: The gate is a desk with a queue behind it, and the register has to be written before the visitor walks in regardless of what the network is doing. Queue it at the node and print the badge from the local series, because an unbadged visitor is somebody the security guard cannot account for at eight in the evening.

closeVisitorPass.because: Signing out happens at the same gate as signing in, at the end of visiting hours, and it is the half of the register that says who is still in the building. Queue it at the node: a pass left open is a receptionist walking the wards looking for somebody who went home an hour ago.

updateBranchSetting.because: Branch settings are the things that differ between sites on purpose — the receipt header, the day-book start, the visiting hours — and the branch that changes one is the branch that has to live with it. Queue it with the version, so two administrators changing different keys merge and the same key is a question rather than a race.

savePlatformSetting.because: A platform setting is hospital-wide configuration — a leave type, an online-appointment rule, a print header — and every branch reads it from the same row. Saving one offline would apply it to one node and to nobody else, which is how two branches end up enforcing two different policies without anyone deciding to.
savePlatformSetting.notes: Deliberately online-only: this row is the single source for every branch, and a queued save would leave one branch running the old policy for however long the uplink is down — a difference nobody would notice until an audit found two answers to one question.

patient.demographic.label: Patient identity
patient.demographic.why: Two desks can both correct a name or an age. Different fields merge; the same field needs a person, because one of the two is wrong and only the patient knows which.

patient.contact.label: Patient contact details
patient.contact.why: Phone numbers change and relatives answer. Different fields merge; the same field is offered to the desk, with both values kept.

appointment.label: Appointment slot
appointment.why: A slot holds one patient. The branch that took the booking owns it, and a second branch asking for the same slot is refused with the alternatives rather than merged.

bed.state.label: Bed state
bed.state.why: A bed holds one patient. Two nodes admitting into the same bed is not a merge — the second arrival needs another bed, so the server refuses the claim.

mar.dose.label: Medication administration
mar.dose.why: A dose is given once. Two nodes signing the same slot is a double-dose risk: the first signature stands and the second is refused with the reason.

admission.label: Admission
admission.why: An admission is an event with a time and an author. Two events on two nodes are two events.

observation.label: Observation set
observation.why: A set of vitals is a measurement at a time. Two sets are two measurements, and both belong on the chart.

nursing.note.label: Nursing note
nursing.note.why: Notes are the record of what was seen and done. Nothing merges and nothing is overwritten.

invoice.label: Invoice
invoice.why: Invoices are reversed and reissued, never edited — so two nodes produce two documents and a credit note, not one merged figure.

payment.label: Payment
payment.why: Money received is a fact with a counter and a time. Two receipts are two payments.

audit.label: Audit entry
audit.why: The ledger of who did what is the one thing that must never be merged away.

ledger.income.label: Income voucher
ledger.income.why: A receipt is money in the drawer at a time and a counter. Nothing merges it and nothing edits it: a correction is a reversing voucher, which is the only form of correction an auditor accepts.

ledger.expense.label: Expense voucher
ledger.expense.why: A payment is money out, with a payee and a cheque or transfer behind it. Two nodes paying the same bill is two payments, and the bank statement will show both.

claim.label: Payer claim
claim.why: One invoice is claimed once with one payer. Two desks submitting the same bill is a duplicate claim, which payers find and hospitals are repaid for by being put on a watch list, so the second submission is refused with the claim number that already holds it.

commission.payout.label: Commission payout
commission.payout.why: A payout is an event: a voucher number, an amount, a withholding, a reference and two names. Nothing about it is edited afterwards — a mistake is corrected by a reversing voucher, and the bank statement shows both.

staff.member.label: Staff record
staff.member.why: Two desks may both correct a designation, a phone number or a bank account. Different fields merge; the same field needs HR, because one of the two values is the one a salary is paid into.

leave.request.label: Leave request
leave.request.why: A leave application is one person’s days, decided once. Two approvers deciding the same application is two answers to one question — the second is refused with the decision already on the record.

attendance.punch.label: Attendance punch
attendance.punch.why: A punch is a fact about a body being in a building at a time. A correction is a second record naming who corrected it and why, never an edit of the first.

payroll.run.label: Payroll run
payroll.run.why: A month is paid once per branch. Two nodes running the same month is two bank files for the same salary, so the second is refused rather than merged.

vital.event.label: Birth or death record
vital.event.why: These are notifications to the state as well as clinical records. Nothing about a birth or a death is edited after the fact: a correction is an amended entry naming what it changes.

visitor.pass.label: Visitor pass
visitor.pass.why: One badge, one visitor, one desk. A visitor who is already inside cannot be signed in again at another desk — the second attempt is refused with the pass that already holds them.

branch.setting.label: Branch setting
branch.setting.why: Two administrators may each change a different branch setting. Different keys merge; the same key needs a person, because the day book and the receipt header cannot read two values.

platform.setting.label: Platform setting
platform.setting.why: Configuration is edited by more than one administrator, and most keys are independent. Different keys merge; the same key is the one case where somebody has to choose, since the next patient sees only one of the two.

applied.meaning: The write is in the canonical record.
applied.client: The outbox entry is dropped and the screen stops marking the row as local.

duplicate.status: 2xx replay, or 409 with problem type dizi.duplicate-operation
duplicate.meaning: This Idempotency-Key was already applied, so nothing changed and the original response is returned.
duplicate.client: The outbox entry is dropped: a drain that ran twice must not write twice.

conflict.meaning: A person has to decide. Both values are returned; nothing is merged silently.
conflict.client: The operation leaves the automatic queue and appears in the review list until someone resolves it.

refused.meaning: The write will never be accepted as it stands.
refused.client: Shown to the desk with the reason and the original entry: retrying it automatically would only hide it.

deferred.meaning: The cloud tier is not reachable, or the server failed in a way that says nothing about the write. A bare 500 is the server’s problem rather than a verdict on the request.
deferred.client: The operation keeps its place in the queue, and the queue keeps its order. Retrying is safe because every queued write carries an Idempotency-Key.

dizi.bed-occupied.title: That bed is already in use
dizi.bed-occupied.when: The bed claim loses to another node
dizi.bed-occupied.client: Send the admission desk back to the bed board; the bed holds one patient

dizi.dose-already-signed.title: This dose has already been signed
dizi.dose-already-signed.when: Two nodes sign the same administration slot
dizi.dose-already-signed.client: Refuse locally and name who signed it and when — this one is a double-dose risk, not a merge

dizi.duplicate-operation.title: This write was already applied
dizi.duplicate-operation.when: The Idempotency-Key has been seen before
dizi.duplicate-operation.client: Treat as success — drop the outbox entry, do not resend

dizi.duplicate-patient.title: This patient may already be registered
dizi.duplicate-patient.when: A registration matches an existing record on the tunable duplicate rules
dizi.duplicate-patient.client: Show the candidates with their evidence; registering anyway needs an acknowledgement

dizi.forbidden.title: Your role cannot do this
dizi.forbidden.when: The token lacks the role the operation needs
dizi.forbidden.client: Hide or disable the action rather than offering it and refusing it

dizi.not-found.title: Not found here
dizi.not-found.when: The record exists on another node or does not exist
dizi.not-found.client: Say which node last saw it when the replica knows — search the branch register, do not dead-end

dizi.number-block-exhausted.title: This node has run out of reserved numbers
dizi.number-block-exhausted.when: A node draws a number with no block left
dizi.number-block-exhausted.client: Stop issuing that series and say so; registering with a made-up number is worse than waiting

dizi.offline-not-allowed.title: This action needs the network
dizi.offline-not-allowed.when: The operation is `online-only` and the cloud tier is unreachable
dizi.offline-not-allowed.client: Explain before the action is attempted, not after — the row shows why it cannot be queued

dizi.slot-taken.title: That slot has just been taken
dizi.slot-taken.when: Another node holds the appointment slot
dizi.slot-taken.client: Offer the alternatives in the response; never silently move the appointment

dizi.stale-version.title: Someone changed this record while you were looking at it
dizi.stale-version.when: The write carries an older `version` than the canonical record
dizi.stale-version.client: Show both values side by side; the desk decides, the server does not guess

dizi.unauthenticated.title: Your session has ended
dizi.unauthenticated.client: Re-authenticate and replay: the outbox survives a session ending

dizi.unavailable.title: The cloud is unreachable
dizi.unavailable.when: The database, or the uplink, or the cloud tier is down
dizi.unavailable.client: Keep the write queued and keep working; the sync pill already says how long it has been

dizi.validation-failed.title: Some fields need attention
dizi.validation-failed.client: Mark the fields from `errors`; keep everything the desk typed

duplicateRules.description: How two records are decided to be the same person. The rule set is data, not code: a branch tunes the weights and the thresholds in Setup, and the register screen and the API read the same set. Two screens checking different rules is how a duplicate comes in through the front door and a false match is flagged at the back. Nothing here merges. A rule can only raise a candidate, and a person decides.
duplicateRules.configuredIn: Setup → Registration → duplicate rules, per branch, with the defaults below. The client reads the weights and the thresholds from here through the generated client, so a branch that tunes them is tuning the one table both the desk form and the import read.
duplicateRules.combination: score = min(1, the sum of the weights of the rules that matched). A rule with `veto: true` is excluded from that sum, and a vetoing match also caps the verdict at `warn`: two records whose sex disagrees are two people, so nothing may be refused on likeness alone. The one exception is the MRN, which is identity rather than likeness — two records carrying one number is a data error and a desk has to look at it whatever else disagrees. At or above `block` the write is refused with 409 and the candidates; at or above `warn` the desk is shown them and may continue; below `warn` nothing is shown, because a desk warned about everything is warned about nothing.

thresholds.note: Raising `block` lets more duplicates through; lowering it starts refusing real new patients, and a phone number shared by a household must never block on its own (0.8 < 0.85) — it warns. One of those is a branch-level judgement, so it belongs to the branch, not to a developer.

rules.label: Same MRN
rules.when: The MRN matches an existing record exactly. This is not a duplicate to review: it is the same patient, so the existing record is opened instead of a second one being created.

rules.label: Same phone number
rules.when: The digits match after stripping spaces, dashes and the country code. A household often shares one number, so this raises a candidate rather than deciding anything.

rules.label: National ID ending matches
rules.when: The last four digits of the national ID match the tail of an existing identifier. A partial match that a complete national-ID field would make unnecessary, kept because the register already contains one.

rules.label: Same name, age and sex
rules.when: Three fields agree. Where names repeat as often as they do here, that is more than a coincidence and still less than a certainty.

rules.label: Same date of birth
rules.when: The full date of birth agrees. Weaker than it looks: the first of January is a placeholder for an unknown date in this register.

rules.label: Name within one edit
rules.when: The names differ by a single insertion, deletion or substitution — the commonest transcription error at a busy desk, and the one a typo-by-typo search never finds.

rules.label: Sex disagrees
rules.when: The records differ on sex, so they are two people. This vetoes a block outright however alike the names look, which is the difference between a duplicate check the desk trusts and one it learns to click past.

conventions.idempotency: Every operation whose `x-dizi.idempotency` is `required` carries an `Idempotency-Key`. A replay of the same key returns the original response and status, so draining a queue twice is safe — which is the whole reason a queue can exist.
conventions.authority: `cloud` means the canonical record lives in the cloud tier and an edge write is a proposal replayed on reconnect. `edge` means the node that owns the record answers: reads come from the replica, and slots belong to the branch that took the booking.
conventions.conflictIsNotAnError: A 409 is a decision for a person, never a failure to hide. The response carries both values and who wrote them, and the app routes it to the review queue rather than retrying in a loop.
conventions.errors: Every failure is RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`. No endpoint returns a bare string or an HTML error page — an offline desk showing `500 Internal Server Error` is a support call.
conventions.audit: Every write marked `audit: true` appends an audit entry in the same transaction as the write. The ledger is hash-chained (P0-208): each entry carries the hash of the previous one on its node’s chain, so an edit in the middle of it is detectable rather than merely discouraged. An offline write carries the node that performed it, so the ledger names the device as well as the person, and the chains are reconciled when the node drains.
conventions.time: Every timestamp is an ISO 8601 instant with an offset. Duration fields hold a duration, never a formatted time — the screens format for Dhaka, the API does not.
